issues: 恒於杖端出過丈六 read as the staff extending beyond the mark; the subject is the Buddha's body, which always rose sixteen feet above the tip of the staff
en_revised: Traveling more than thirty *li* eastward through the empty valleys of Buddhavana Mountain (Skt. *buddha-vana*), one reaches Yaṣṭivana (洩瑟知林) (洩 is pronounced y[i] + [j]ie) (in the language of Tang, this means "Staff Forest"). The forest’s bamboo is tall and slender, covering the mountains and filling the valleys. Long ago, there was a Brahmin who heard that the body of the Buddha Śākyamuni was sixteen feet tall; he constantly harbored doubts and, unable to believe it, took a sixteen-foot bamboo staff, intending to measure the Buddha’s body. The Buddha's body always rose sixteen feet above the tip of the staff; as it continued to grow taller in this way, he could never reach the truth of it, so he threw the staff away and departed, and it subsequently took root. Within the forest is a large *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here manifesting great supernatural powers for the sake of gods and humans, and expounding the profound and subtle Dharma.  Recently, in the Staff Forest, there was an *upāsaka* named Jayasena (in the language of Tang, this means "Victorious Army"), who belonged to the Kṣatriya caste of Western India. His aspirations were for simplicity and ease, his heart delighted in the mountains and forests, and while his physical traces remained in this illusory realm, his mind roamed the boundaries of ultimate truth. He had thoroughly investigated the subtle mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, possessing noble eloquence and elegant manners. Śramaṇas, Brahmins, followers of non-Buddhist paths, heterodox scholars, kings, ministers, elders, and the wealthy and influential all flocked to visit him, bowing their heads to request instruction. Of every ten households, six had sent disciples to receive his instruction. Now approaching seventy years of age, he studied with tireless devotion; having abandoned all other arts, he practiced only the Buddhist scriptures, exerting his body and mind without ceasing day or night. According to the custom of India, scented powder is mixed into clay to make small stupas five or six inches high; scriptures are written and placed inside them, which are called Dharma relics. As the number gradually accumulates, a large stupa is built to house them all within, where offerings are constantly performed. Thus, the practice of Jayasena (勝軍) was as follows: his mouth would proclaim the wonderful Dharma to guide and encourage students, while his hands would make stupas to cultivate superior merit. At night, he would practice circumambulation, chanting, and seated meditation, never finding time for sleep or food, and working day and night without slackening. He reached one hundred years of age, yet his resolve and work did not decline. Over a period of thirty years, he made a total of seven koṭis (in the Tang language, *yi* [億]) of Dharma-relic stupas. Each time he completed one koṭi, he built a large stupa to house them all, where he grandly performed offerings and invited the monastic assembly to celebrate with a religious ceremony. At those times, a divine light would shine brilliantly as a manifest miracle, and from then on, it would emit light from time to time.
li_quote: the Buddha’s height always exceeded the length of the stick by sixteen feet

issues: 兩三月 read as "two or three months": 兩 here is 雨 (the text's own idiom 唯雨三月，多雨不行 at 05.01; Li 雨三月; as 兩安居 = 雨安居 at 07.01.10, 08.06.30): the three months of the rains No edition is recorded with 雨 here (no Taishō apparatus note; the Sixi print lacks juan 9, the Jōō print is unclear); the reading follows the idiom and the Song 雨 at 09.02.16.
en_revised: Traveling six or seven li southeast from the Yaṣṭi Wood (杖林), one reaches a great mountain. In front of a transverse ridge stands a stone stupa where the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma to humans and devas for the three months of the rains. At that time, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王), wishing to come and hear the Dharma, cleared the mountain and piled up stones to build a staircase for his ascent, measuring over twenty paces in width and three or four li in length.

issues: 此比丘遙覩聖眾: 聖眾 is the holy assembly (the Buddha with his monks), not 'the Holy One'; and the one who 即昇虛空 after the Buddha's words is the bhikṣu, not the Buddha
en_revised: To the left of the north gate of the mountain city, on the shaded side of the southern cliff, traveling east for two or three li, one arrives at a great stone chamber; in the past, Devadatta entered into meditation here. Not far to the east of the stone chamber, there are colored streaks on a flat rock that appear as if stained with blood, and beside it stands a stūpa built at the place where a bhikṣu practicing meditation took his own life and attained the fruit of sainthood. Formerly, there was a bhikṣu who exerted his mind and body, living in seclusion to practice meditation; as the years passed, he did not attain the holy fruit. Retiring and blaming himself, he sighed privately, saying: "The fruit of the non-learner (aśaikṣa) is not attained in time; what is the use of living in this body burdened with defilements!" He then went to this rock and stabbed his own neck; at that moment, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, rose into the void, manifested spiritual transformations, transformed into fire to consume his body, and entered into extinction (parinirvāṇa). Admiring his noble conduct, they built this to record his merit. On the cliff to the east of where the bhikṣu attained the fruit, there is a stone stūpa at the place where a bhikṣu practicing meditation threw himself from the cliff and attained the fruit of sainthood. Formerly, in the time of the Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who sat in the mountain forests practicing the meditation for attaining the fruit; though he had been diligent for a long time, he could not realize the fruit, yet he continued his contemplation day and night without forgetting his tranquil meditation. The Tathāgata, knowing that his faculties were about to ripen, went there to bring it to completion; he traveled from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana) to the foot of the mountain cliff, snapped his fingers to summon him, and stood waiting. Seeing the holy assembly from afar, the bhikṣu felt great joy in body and mind and threw himself from the cliff; because of his pure heart and his respectful faith in the Buddha's words, he attained the fruit of sainthood before reaching the ground. The World-Honored One said, "You should know that now is the time." The bhikṣu then ascended into the void and manifested miraculous transformations. This was to make manifest his pure faith, and therefore this memorial was established.
li_quote: Seeing the holy monks from a distance, the bhikṣu was encouraged and jumped down the cliff with delight.

issues: 兩三月 read as "two or three months": 兩 here is 雨 (the text's own idiom 唯雨三月，多雨不行 at 05.01; Li 雨三月; as 兩安居 = 雨安居 at 07.01.10, 08.06.30): the three months of the rains
en_revised: Traveling five or six li southwest from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana), on the northern side of the South Mountain (Dakṣiṇagiri), in a great bamboo forest, there is a large stone chamber. This is where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with nine hundred and ninety great arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka after the Tathāgata’s nirvana. In front are the old foundations of a hall built by King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) for the great arhats who were to compile the Dharma-treasury.  Initially, while Mahākāśyapa was sitting in meditation in the mountain forest, he suddenly saw a brilliant light and observed the earth quake. He said, "What omen is this, that it should be so extraordinary?" Using his heavenly eye to observe, he saw that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvana between the twin trees, and he immediately ordered his followers to hasten to the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城). On the road, he met a Brahman holding a heavenly flower in his hand. Mahākāśyapa asked, "Where do you come from? Do you know where my Great Teacher is now?" The Brahman replied, "I have just come from that city of Kuśinagara; I saw that your Great Teacher has already entered nirvana, and the multitudes of gods and men are all making offerings. The flower I hold was obtained from there."  Upon hearing this, Mahākāśyapa said to his followers, "The sun of wisdom has set, the world is in darkness, the excellent guide has departed, and sentient beings will fall into ruin." Lax monks congratulated one another, saying, "The Tathāgata has attained extinction, so we are now at ease. If we commit any offense, who will be able to rebuke or restrain us?" Hearing this, Mahākāśyapa was deeply saddened and thought to compile the Dharma-treasury to govern offenses according to the teachings. He then went to the twin trees to view the transformation and pay his respects. Soon after, the Dharma King passed away, leaving humans and gods without a guide, and the great arhats also entered parinirvāṇa. At that time, Mahākāśyapa thought to himself, "In obedience to the Buddha’s teachings, it is appropriate to compile the Dharma-treasury." Thereupon, he ascended Mount Sumeru (蘇迷盧山), struck the great ghaṇṭā (大揵稚), and proclaimed: "A Dharma assembly is about to be held in the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城); all those who have realized the fruits of the path should assemble here with haste!" The sound of the ghaṇṭā carried the teaching of Kāśyapa, reaching throughout the trichiliomegachiliocosm, and all who possessed supernatural powers heard it and gathered.  At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the assembly, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered extinction, and the world is empty. We must compile the Dharma-treasury to repay the Buddha’s kindness. Now, in compiling the Dharma, we must prioritize simplicity and quietude; how could we rely on a large crowd and fail to accomplish this noble task? Those who possess the three knowledges (三明), have attained the six supernatural powers (六通), are endowed with perfect retention (聞持) without error, and possess unobstructed eloquence (辯才)—such superior persons may participate in the compilation. All the rest, those who hold a fruit and those still in training, should return to their respective dwellings."  Thus, he obtained nine hundred and ninety people, excluding Ānanda, who was still in the stage of learning. Mahākāśyapa summoned him and said, "You have not yet exhausted the outflows (漏); you should leave the assembly of sages." Ānanda replied, "I have attended upon the Tathāgata for many years, and whenever there were discussions on the Dharma, I was never excluded. Now that the compilation is to take place, I am being expelled; the Dharma King has entered extinction, and I have lost my refuge." Kāśyapa told him, "Do not harbor sorrow or distress. Although you have personally attended upon the Buddha and are indeed learned, your attachments and delusions have not yet been exhausted, and your habitual bonds have not yet been severed." Ānanda, silenced, withdrew and went to a quiet, secluded place, desiring to attain the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), but despite his diligent efforts, he did not attain it. Having become exhausted and weary, he intended to lie down for a moment; before his head had even touched the pillow, he attained the state of an Arhat. He went to the place of the assembly and knocked on the door to announce his arrival. Kāśyapa asked, "Have you exhausted your defilements? You should employ your supernatural powers and enter without using the door." Ānanda accepted the command, entered through the keyhole, paid homage to the monks, and then withdrew to sit down. This was on the fifteenth day, the beginning of the summer retreat.  Thereupon, Kāśyapa proclaimed aloud, "Reflect and listen carefully! Ānanda, who has heard and retained the teachings, and whom the Tathāgata praised, shall compile the Sūtra-piṭaka (素呾纜藏) (formerly called *xiuduoluo* [修多羅], which is erroneous). Upāli, who is clear and thorough in upholding the Vinaya and is recognized by the assembly, shall compile the Vinaya-piṭaka (毘奈耶藏) (formerly called *pinaye* [毘那耶], which is erroneous). I, Kāśyapa, shall compile the Abhidharma-piṭaka." When the three months of the rains were over, the compilation of the three piṭakas was completed. Because Mahākāśyapa was the senior elder (sthavira) among the monks, it was consequently called the Sthavira school (Sthaviravāda).  To the northwest of where Mahākāśyapa held the assembly, there is a stūpa; this is where Ānanda, having been rebuked by the monks and excluded from the assembly, came to sit in meditation and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Only after attaining this fruit was he permitted to participate.

issues: 如來於此說法及度羅怙羅: 度 is to ordain (admit into the order), not 'converted'
en_revised: Not far to the northeast of the stone pillar, one reaches the city of Rājagṛha (曷羅闍姞利呬城) (in the language of Tang, "King's Abode" [王舍]). The outer wall has already collapsed, and no remains of the ramparts are left; although the inner city is ruined, its foundations are still steep and high, measuring over twenty *li* in circumference, with one gate on each side.   Formerly, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) had his capital in the Upper Palace City, the households of the registered inhabitants frequently suffered from the calamity of fire. If one family was negligent, the neighbors on all four sides would suffer the disaster; the people had no time for anything but fire prevention, their properties and livelihoods were abandoned, and the masses lived in grievance and unrest. The king said, "Because of my lack of virtue, the common people suffer; what merit can I cultivate to avert this?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous transformation is harmonious and peaceful, and your governance and teachings are clear and discerning. Now, these common people are not cautious, leading to these fires. It is appropriate to establish strict regulations to prevent future offenses. If a fire breaks out, investigate thoroughly to find who started it, punish the primary culprit, and banish them to the Cold Forest (寒林)."   The Cold Forest is a place where corpses are abandoned; it is commonly called an inauspicious place, and people avoid traveling there. "Now, to banish them there is the same as treating them like a corpse. Since they will be ashamed of such a lowly dwelling, they will naturally be cautious and protective." The king said, "Good; it should be announced everywhere to the residents." Shortly after, a fire broke out in the king’s own palace first. He said to his ministers, "I shall move." He then ordered the crown prince to oversee the affairs of the capital, and wishing to clarify the laws of the state, he moved his residence there. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐王), hearing that King Bimbisāra was living in the open at the Cold Forest, assembled his troops with the intent to launch a surprise attack. The border guards reported this, and he then built a city. Because the king had first taken up residence here, it was called Rājagṛha (the City of the King’s Abode). The officials, the gentry, and the common people all moved their households there. Some say that it was not until King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) that this city was built; once the crown prince Ajātaśatru succeeded to the throne, he then made it his capital. By the time King Aśoka (無憂王) moved the capital to Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐城), he bestowed Rājagṛha upon the brahmans; therefore, there are no longer any common people in the city, only fewer than a thousand brahman families. In the southwest corner of the palace city are two small saṃghārāmas where visiting monks from various countries stay when they come and go; this is the place where the Buddha formerly expounded the Dharma. To the northwest of this is a stūpa, the former birthplace of the elder Jyotiṣka (珠底色迦) (in the language of Tang, "Star Calendar" [星曆]; formerly called Shutijia [樹提伽], which is erroneous). Outside the south gate of the city, to the left of the road, there is a stūpa where the Tathāgata expounded the Dharma and ordained Rāhula.
li_quote: a stupa at the spot where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma and ordained Rāhula

issues: 中路 is 'midway along the road (up the mountain)', not 'the middle path'
en_revised: Midway along the road there are two small stūpas: one is called "Dismounting" (Xiàchéng 下乘), marking the place where the king would arrive and proceed on foot; the other is called "Turning Back the Ordinary" (Tuìfán 退凡), marking where ordinary people were screened and not permitted to go further.
li_quote: There are two small stupas on the way.

issues: 十億金錢 is ten koṭis (億 = koṭi, cf. 拘胝（唐言億）), not 'ten billion'; 逾千載而彌隆 is 'it will flourish ever more for over a thousand years', not 'after a thousand years'; 智月 is Jñānacandra, not Candrakīrti (月稱)
en_revised: From here, traveling north for more than thirty *li*, one arrives at the Nālandā (translated into Chinese as "Giving Without Weariness") monastery. I heard from the elders that in the mango grove to the south of this monastery there is a pond; a dragon named Nālandā lived there, and because the monastery was built beside it, it took its name from the dragon. According to the actual account, it is because the Tathāgata, in the past when practicing the bodhisattva path, was a great king who established his capital in this place. He felt compassion for sentient beings and delighted in giving generously; at the time, people praised his virtue and called him "Giving Without Weariness," and thus the monastery took this as its name. The land was originally a mango grove; five hundred merchants bought it with ten koṭis of gold coins and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma here for three months, and the merchants all attained the fruits of sainthood. Not long after the Buddha’s nirvana, a former king of this country named Śakrāditya (translated into Chinese as "Emperor Sun" [帝日]) deeply respected the One Vehicle and honored the Triple Gem; he selected this auspicious site by divination and built this monastery. When the work first began, they pierced and injured the body of the dragon. At that time, there was a Nirgrantha outsider skilled in divination who saw this and predicted: "This is a superior site; if a monastery is built here, it will surely flourish and become the standard for the five Indias. It will grow ever more prosperous for more than a thousand years, and later students will easily complete their studies here. However, there will be much coughing of blood, because the dragon was injured." His son, King Buddhagupta (translated into Chinese as "Protector of Awakening"), succeeded to the throne and, following the noble legacy, built another monastery to the south of this one. King Tathāgatagupta (translated into Chinese as "Thus-Come") earnestly followed the noble legacy and built another monastery to the east of this one. When King Bālāditya (translated into Chinese as "Young Sun") succeeded to the throne, he built another monastery to the northeast of this one. When the work was completed and the ceremonies finished, he held a celebratory feast of merit, expressing his sincerity to both the hidden and the manifest, and invited both the ordinary and the holy. At this assembly, monks from the five Indias gathered from ten thousand miles away. Once the assembly was seated, two monks arrived late and were led up to the third-story pavilion. Someone asked, "The King is holding this assembly and has invited the ordinary and the holy; from what place do you venerable ones come, that you arrive last?" They replied, "We have come from the country of Cīna (至那國); our teacher was suffering from an illness, so we departed only after he had eaten. Having received the King’s distant invitation, we have come to attend the assembly." The questioner was astonished and immediately reported this to the King. The King, knowing in his heart that they were sages, went in person to inquire of them, but when he arrived at the upper pavilion, he did not know where they had gone. The King’s faith deepened further, and he renounced his kingdom to become a monk. Once he had become a monk, he was ranked at the very end of the assembly, which left him constantly dissatisfied and uneasy, thinking: "I was once a king, occupying the highest and most honorable position; now that I have become a monk, I am ranked at the very end of the assembly." He soon went to inform the monks and recounted his situation. Thereupon, the assembly of monks reached a consensus, decreeing that those who have not yet received the full precepts shall be ranked according to their age; thus, this monastery alone possesses this rule. The King’s son, Vajra (translated into Chinese as "Diamond"), possessed a firm and steadfast faith; after succeeding to the throne, he built another monastery to the west of this site. Afterward, the King of Central India built another great monastery to the north of this one. Thereupon, the surrounding walls were raised high, and they were joined into a single gate; since successive kings have built them generation after generation, exhausting all the arts of carving and joinery, it is truly a magnificent sight. In the original great monastery of Śakrāditya (帝日), a Buddha image is now installed, and forty monks are dispatched from the assembly daily to eat here in order to repay the kindness of the donors. The number of monks is several thousand, all of whom are men of outstanding talent and high learning; those whose virtue is esteemed in the present age and whose fame has spread to foreign lands number more than several hundred. Their conduct in the precepts is pure and white, and their monastic discipline is refined and perfect; the monks have strict regulations, and the assembly is entirely upright and simple, such that all the countries of India look to them as a model. They seek instruction and discuss profound mysteries, finding the whole day insufficient; they remain vigilant and admonish one another day and night, with the old and young helping each other to perfection, and if there were any who did not discuss the subtle meanings of the Tripitaka, they would feel ashamed of their own shadows. Therefore, scholars from foreign lands who wish to spread their reputation all come here to resolve their doubts, and only then does their elegant fame flow forth. For this reason, even those who travel about falsely claiming its name are everywhere treated with respect. When those from distant regions and foreign lands wish to enter for discussion, the gatekeepers pose difficult questions, and many are forced to turn back; only those who are deeply learned in both ancient and modern studies are permitted to enter. Consequently, when visiting scholars and newcomers discuss their arts and abilities in detail, those who are forced to retreat are certainly seven or eight out of every ten. As for the few who are broadly learned, they are questioned in turn by the assembly, and there is none whose sharpness is not blunted and whose reputation is not diminished. As for those of eminent talent and broad learning, possessing strong memories and many abilities, these virtuous and wise men join their brilliance and follow in the footsteps of their predecessors. As for Dharmapāla (護法) and Candrapāla (護月), they stirred the fragrant dust of the Buddha’s legacy; Guṇamati (德慧) and Sthiramati (堅慧) spread their elegant reputations throughout their time; there were the refined discourses of Prabhāmitra (光友) and the lofty discussions of Jinamitra (勝友); Jñānacandra (智月) was clear and keen in his discernment; and Śīlabhadra (戒賢) possessed virtue that was sublime and profound. These superior men were known to all; their virtue excelled that of their predecessors, and their learning encompassed the ancient texts; each composed more than ten treatises and commentaries, which were widely circulated and highly valued by their contemporaries. Around the monastery, there are hundreds of sacred traces; I shall cite two or three of them as a brief summary.
li_quote: purchased it with ten koṭis of gold coins … It will continue to thrive for more than a thousand years … Jñānacandra of elegant demeanor and perspicacious discernment

issues: 世尊遙見，指告眾曰：彼來者，我弟子中神足第一…善來，比丘…鬚髮落: the prediction and ordination concern Maudgalyāyana alone (彼來者 'that one coming', 比丘 singular), not his whole company; plurals ('Those who are coming are the foremost', 'Welcome, monks', 'their hair…their defilements') corrected to the singular
en_revised: Traveling eight or nine li southwest from the monastery, one reaches the town of Kolika (拘理迦邑), where there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is the native village of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子). Beside it is a stūpa marking the place where the Venerable One entered the nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), and it contains his bodily relics. The Venerable One was of a great Brahmin lineage and had been a close friend of Śāriputra since youth. Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent, while the Venerable One was renowned for his profound discernment; they were equals in wisdom, always together in their movements, bound by a lifelong pact to share the same path, and together they grew weary of the secular world and sought to leave the householder's life, eventually taking Sañjaya as their teacher. Śāriputra encountered the arhat Aśvajit, heard the Dharma, and attained realization; he returned and recounted it to the Venerable One, who, upon hearing and realizing the Dharma, attained the first fruit. Together with his two hundred and fifty disciples, he went to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw him from afar and, pointing him out to the assembly, said: "That one who is coming will be the foremost in supernatural powers among my disciples." Upon arriving at the place of the Buddha, he requested to enter the Dharma. The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, bhikṣu; practice the holy life purely to reach the end of suffering." Upon hearing these words, his hair and beard fell away, his secular garments changed, his precepts became pure, and his deportment became harmonious. After seven days, his defilements were exhausted, he attained the fruit of arhatship, and he gained supernatural powers. Three or four li to the east of the native village of Maudgalyāyana, there is a stūpa at the place where King Bimbisāra went to meet and see the Buddha. When the Tathāgata first realized the fruit of buddhahood, he knew that the hearts of the people in the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) were thirsting with longing. He accepted the invitation of King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) and, in the early morning, donned his robes and took up his alms bowl. Surrounded on all sides by a thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were elder brahmans with shell-shaped topknots who had donned dyed robes out of admiration for the Dharma, following him in his retinue—he entered the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). At that time, the heavenly king Śakra (帝釋天王) transformed himself into a māṇava (摩那婆) with a shell-shaped topknot on his head. Holding a golden vase in his left hand and a precious staff in his right, his feet treading on empty space four finger-widths above the ground, he led the way for the Buddha amidst the assembly. Then King Bimbisāra of the country of Magadha, together with the various brahmans, elders, and laypeople of his kingdom—a multitude of hundreds of thousands—came out of the city of Rājagṛha in a procession to welcome the holy assembly.
li_quote: When the World-honored One saw him from a distance he pointed at the newcomer and told the assembly of monks, “That person coming from over there will become the disciple most notable for his miraculous powers.”

issues: 斯則王化所由，國風尚學 says the monk's zeal is owing to his king's transforming influence and his country's love of learning; read as 'This is the source of royal transformation and the reason why…'
en_revised: From here, traveling east for over nine hundred li and crossing a great river, one reaches the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國) (in the territory of East India). The country of Kāmarūpa is over ten thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over thirty li in circuit. The land is low and moist, and crops are sown at the proper seasons. Although there are many *panasa* (般核娑 - jackfruit) and *nārikela* (那羅雞羅 - coconut) trees, they are considered very precious. Rivers, lakes, and ponds encircle the cities and towns. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. The people are short in stature and dark in complexion. Their language differs slightly from that of Central India. Their nature is very fierce and impetuous, but they are determined to study diligently. They revere and serve the heavenly gods and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, from the time the Buddha appeared until the present, no monasteries have been built to gather monks. Those who have pure faith only pay homage in secret. There are several hundred deva temples and tens of thousands of non-Buddhists. The reigning king is a descendant of the god Nārāyaṇa and belongs to the Brahman caste; his name is Bhāskaravarman (婆塞羯羅伐摩) (in the language of Tang, "Sun-Armor"), and his title is Kumāra (拘摩羅) (in the language of Tang, "Youth"). Since he first occupied this territory, his family has ruled for a thousand generations down to the present king. The king is fond of learning, and the common people follow his example; men of high talent from distant lands, admiring his righteousness, come to travel as his guests. Although he does not sincerely believe in the Buddha-dharma, he respects learned śramaṇas. Previously, having heard that a śramaṇa from the country of Cīna (至那國) was at the Nālandā (那爛陀) Monastery in Magadha, having come from afar to study the profound Dharma of the Buddha, the king sent cordial invitations back and forth three times, but the monk had not yet complied with the request. At that time, the Master of Treatises Śīlabhadra (尸羅跋陀羅) said, "If you wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness, you must propagate the True Dharma. You should go; do not fear the long journey. The family of King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) has followed non-Buddhist paths for generations, and his invitation to a śramaṇa is a virtuous deed. If he changes his course because of this, the benefits will be vast and far-reaching. You previously aroused a great mind and made a grand vow, wishing to travel alone to foreign lands, casting aside your body to seek the Dharma and universally save all sentient beings—how could this be limited to your own country? You should forget about gain and loss, disregard honor and disgrace, propagate the holy teachings, enlighten the deluded, put others before yourself, and forget personal fame to spread the Dharma."  Thereupon, being unable to decline, he accompanied the envoy and went to meet him. King Kumāra said, "Although I am without talent, I have always admired those of high learning. Having heard of your fame and noble character, I ventured to invite you." He replied, "I am of little ability and narrow wisdom, yet I have undeservedly received your attention."  King Kumāra said, "Excellent! You admire the Dharma and love learning, regarding your own body as light as a feather, crossing heavy dangers to travel far to foreign lands. This is owing to the transforming influence of your king and to the custom of your country of valuing learning. Now, in all the countries of India, there are many who sing the 'Music of the King of Qin Breaking the Battle Lines' (秦王破陣樂) of the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國); I have heard it for a long time. Is this not the country of the Great Virtuous One?" He replied, "Indeed, this song praises the virtues of my sovereign."  King Kumāra said, "I did not realize that you, Great Virtuous One, were a man of this country. I have always admired its refined culture and have long looked toward the East, but as the mountains and rivers block the way, I have had no means to go there myself." I replied, "The sacred virtues of our great monarch spread far and wide, and his benevolent influence reaches distant lands; those from foreign regions with different customs who come to the imperial palace to pay homage and declare themselves subjects are numerous indeed." King Kumāra said, "Since his grace covers all like heaven and earth, I have long hoped to send tribute. Now King Śīlāditya (戒日王) is in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國), where he is about to hold a great almsgiving to cultivate merit and wisdom; all the Śramaṇas and Brahmins of the five Indias who possess learning have been summoned to assemble. He has now sent an envoy to invite me, and I wish for you to travel with me." I therefore went with him.  In the eastern part of this country, mountains and hills are interconnected, and there are no large capital cities; as its borders adjoin the Southwest Yi (西南夷), its people resemble the Man (蠻) and Lao (獠) tribes. I inquired in detail about the local customs and learned that one could reach the southwestern borders of Shu (蜀) in about two months' travel; however, the mountains and rivers are treacherous and obstructed, the mountain mists are noxious, and poisonous snakes and herbs cause great harm. In the southeast of the country, wild elephants roam in violent herds, which is why the elephant corps of this country is particularly numerous.
li_quote: This was due to the ediﬁcation of your king and the result of the general mood of advocating learning in your country.

en_revised: The country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) is over 7,000 li in circumference. The capital city is over 40 li in circumference. The land is fertile, the climate is warm and hot, crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The population is prosperous, and the households are wealthy. The people are short and dark-skinned, and their temperaments are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and value virtue, honoring goodness and diligently cultivating merit. This country was originally an island of gems; it contains many precious treasures and is inhabited by ghosts and spirits.  Later, there was a king in South India whose daughter was betrothed to a neighboring country. On an auspicious day, as she was being escorted there, they encountered a lion on the road. Her attendants abandoned the girl and fled to escape the danger, but the girl remained in her carriage, resigned to losing her life. At that time, the lion king carried the girl away, entering deep mountains and dwelling in secluded valleys. He hunted deer and gathered fruit to provide for her in due season. After many years had passed, she gave birth to a son and a daughter; their appearance was that of humans, but their nature was that of beasts.   As the son gradually grew up, he had the strength to wrestle with wild beasts. When he reached the age of twenty, his human intelligence began to manifest, and he said to his mother, "What am I? My father is a wild beast, and my mother is a human. Since we are not of the same species, how could they have mated?" His mother then recounted the past to her son. He said, "Humans and beasts follow different paths; we should flee at once." The mother said, "I tried to escape before, but I could not succeed on my own." The son subsequently followed his lion father, climbing mountains and crossing ridges to observe his movements so that they might escape the danger. Once he had waited for his father to leave, he carried his mother and sister on his back and descended toward human settlements. The mother said, "We must each be cautious and secretive; do not speak of the origin of these events, for if people should hear of them, they may look down upon us." Thereupon, they arrived at her father’s native country, but the country was not that of their kin, and their ancestral line had already been extinguished. They sought shelter with the townspeople, who asked them, "From what country are you?" They replied, "We are originally from this country, but we were scattered in foreign lands; mother and son have traveled together to return to our old home." The people all felt pity and compassion, and together they provided them with supplies.  When the lion king returned and saw nothing, he pined for his children. His fury erupted, and he left the mountain valleys to roam among the villages and towns, roaring and thundering, violently harming people and animals, and cruelly destroying living beings. Whenever the townspeople came out, he would seize and kill them. They beat drums and blew conch shells, shouldered crossbows and held spears, and followed in groups like an army; only then could they avoid harm.  The king, fearing that his benevolent influence was not reaching the people, released hunters, hoping to capture the beast. The king personally led the four divisions of the army, numbering in the tens of thousands, to surround the forests and thickets, spanning across the mountains and valleys. The lion roared, and both men and beasts fled in terror. Since he could not be captured, the king subsequently issued a recruitment call: whoever could seize the lion and rid the country of this menace would be rewarded with a great prize to honor their distinguished achievement.  Upon hearing the king’s order, the son said to his mother, "Our hunger and cold have become extreme; I should respond to the recruitment, for perhaps I may gain something with which to support you." The mother said, "You must not speak like this! Although he is a beast, he is still called your father; how could you, because of hardship, commit such an act of rebellion and harm?" The son replied, "Humans and beasts are of different species; where then is the place for ritual and righteousness? Since we are already obstructed and hindered, what hope is there for this heart?" He then hid a small knife in his sleeve and went out to answer the recruitment. At that time, thousands of people and ten thousand cavalry gathered like clouds and mist, but the lion sat in the forest, and no one dared to approach. The son went directly before him, and the father became tame and submissive. Thus, out of affection, he forgot his anger; the son then stabbed his blade into the father’s belly. The father still harbored loving kindness and remained without resentment or malice, even as his belly was ripped open, and he died enduring the pain. The king asked, "What kind of person is this, that he is so extraordinary?" He tempted him with benefits and threatened him with punishment, after which the son fully explained the beginning and the end, detailing the entire situation. The king said, "How rebellious! If he would even harm his own father, how much more so would he harm those who are not his kin? The beast species is difficult to tame, and their violent nature is easily stirred. To remove a menace to the people is a great merit, but to sever the life of one's father is a rebellious heart. I shall provide a heavy reward to compensate for his merit, but I shall banish him far away to punish his rebellion. In this way, the laws of the country will not be compromised, and the king’s word will not be inconsistent." Thereupon, he fitted out two large ships and stored them with plenty of provisions. The mother was left in the country and provided for with the reward for the merit, while the son and daughter were each placed on a ship and left to drift with the waves. The son’s ship drifted across the sea until it reached this island of treasures; seeing an abundance of precious gems, he settled there. Later, when merchants came to the island to collect treasures, he killed the merchant leader and kept their women. In this way they multiplied, and their descendants were numerous. They then established a ruler and ministers, assigned ranks of high and low, built a capital and cities, and occupied the territory. Because their ancestor had captured a lion (siṃha), they cited this original achievement to name the country. As for the ship carrying the daughter, it drifted to the west of Persia (Pārasī), where she was bewitched by spirits and gave birth to a group of daughters; this is the origin of the present-day Western Kingdom of Women. Therefore, the people of the country of the Lion (Siṃhala) are short and dark in appearance, with square chins and broad foreheads; their temperament is fierce and violent, and they are cruel and prone to poisoning. This is because they are the descendants of a wild beast, and thus the people are mostly brave and robust. This is one account.  What the Buddha’s teaching records is as follows: In the past, in the great iron city of this precious island, there dwelt five hundred rākṣasīs. Atop the city towers, two tall banners were erected to signify signs of good or ill fortune; the auspicious banner would move when there was a lucky event, and the inauspicious banner would move when there was a calamity. They would constantly lie in wait for merchants arriving at the precious island, whereupon they would transform into beautiful women, carrying fragrant flowers and playing music to welcome and console them, luring them into the iron city. After the festivities and banquets were over, they would place the merchants in an iron prison and gradually devour them.  At that time, in the continent of Jambudvīpa, there was a great merchant leader named Saṃgha; his son was named Saṃghala. His father being old, he took over the family business and set out with five hundred merchants to enter the sea to collect treasures. Blown about by wind and waves, they happened to reach the precious island. When the rākṣasīs saw the auspicious banner move, they brought fragrant flowers and played music, coming together to welcome the merchants and entice them into the iron city. The merchant leader then engaged in joyful entertainment with the rākṣasī queen, and the remaining merchants each paired off with one, and as the years passed, they all fathered children. The rākṣasīs, their affections for their old partners having grown distant, wished to imprison them in an iron jail to wait for other merchants. At that time, Saṃghala had a nightmare during the night and, knowing it was not an auspicious sign, secretly sought a path home. He happened upon the iron jail and heard the sound of piteous wailing, so he climbed a tall tree and asked, "Who is it that is bound and suffering such grief?" They replied, "Do you not know? The women in the city are all rākṣasīs. In the past, they enticed us into the city for entertainment. Once you had arrived, they imprisoned us and gradually consumed us as food; now more than half are gone, and before long, you too will suffer this same calamity." Saṃghala asked, "What plan can be devised to escape this danger?" They replied, "We have heard that there is a heavenly horse on the seashore; if one prays with utmost sincerity, it will surely ferry one across to safety." Having heard this, Saṃghala secretly informed the other merchants, and together they looked toward the seashore, focusing their minds on seeking salvation. At that time, the heavenly horse came and told the men, "If each of you grasps my mane and does not look back, I will ferry you across the sea to escape this peril and reach the continent of Jambudvīpa, returning to your home country." The merchants followed these instructions with single-minded devotion and gripped its mane; the heavenly horse then soared into the clouds and galloped across the seacoast. The rākṣasīs (羅剎女) suddenly realized their husbands had fled; they told one another, wondering where they had gone, and each carrying her young child, they flew through the air in search of them. Knowing the merchants were about to reach the seashore, they called out to one another and flew off to find them. Before long, they encountered the company of merchants; with mixed feelings of grief and joy, their tears flowed freely as they covered their faces, sobbing and saying: "I am grateful for our meeting and fortunate to have wed such a fine man; our home was full of joy and we have long shared deep affection, yet now you abandon us to go far away, leaving your wife and child desolate—how can anyone endure such a heart-wrenching fate? We pray you, look back and return with us to the city."  The hearts of the merchants remained unmoved. The rākṣasīs, finding their entreaties of no avail, resorted to their demonic charms and employed every manner of deception. The merchants, overcome by love and unable to bear the separation, felt their resolve waver, and they all fell back. The rākṣasīs congratulated one another and went away, holding the merchants by the hand.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅), however, possessed deep and firm wisdom; his mind was free from attachments, and he succeeded in crossing the great sea, escaping this peril. Meanwhile, the queen of the rākṣasīs returned alone to the Iron City. The other rākṣasīs said to her, "You lack wisdom and strategy, having been abandoned by your husband; since you are devoid of skill and ability, you should no longer dwell here."  The queen of the rākṣasīs then took the child she had borne, flew before Siṃhala, and, exerting her utmost charms, enticed and pleaded with him to return. Siṃhala recited a mantra and, brandishing his sharp sword, rebuked her, saying: "You are a rākṣasī, and I am a human; humans and ghosts follow different paths, and we are not a match. If you press me hard, I shall end your life." The rākṣasī, knowing that her seduction had failed, flew through the air and arrived at the home of Siṃhala (僧伽羅). She deceived his father, Siṃha (僧伽), saying: "I am the daughter of a certain king. Siṃhala took me as his wife and we bore a son. We were carrying precious goods to return to his native country, but while crossing the sea, we encountered a storm and our ship was wrecked. Only my son, myself, and Siṃhala managed to survive. The mountains and rivers were difficult to traverse, and we suffered from cold, hunger, and hardship. Because of one word that displeased him, I was abandoned and cast aside, insulted with improper language, and reviled as a rākṣasī. To return home is to face a vast distance, and to stay here is to be a lonely, stranded traveler. With nowhere to turn, I dare to present my situation."  Siṃha said, "It is truly as you say; you should enter the house at once." Not long after, Siṃhala arrived. His father said to him, "Why do you value wealth and treasure while slighting your wife and child?" Siṃhala replied, "This is a rākṣasī." He then explained the previous events in detail to his parents, and his relatives and kin all joined in driving her away.  The rākṣasī then complained to the king, and the king wished to punish Siṃhala. Siṃhala said, "She is a rākṣasī, and her nature is full of seductive bewitchment." The king believed this was untrue, and being charmed by her beauty, he said to Siṃhala, "If you must abandon this woman, I shall keep her in my harem." Siṃhala replied, "I fear it will bring disaster. Since she is a rākṣasī, her only food is blood and flesh." The king did not listen to the words of Siṃhala and proceeded to take her as his wife. Later, in the middle of the night, she flew back to the precious island (Ratnadvīpa) and summoned the other five hundred rākṣasī demonesses to come together to the royal palace. Using poisonous incantations, they ravaged the palace; they ate the flesh and drank the blood of all the people and animals, then took the remaining corpses and returned to the precious island. At daybreak, the ministers and officials gathered for court, but the palace gates were closed and would not open. They waited and listened for a long time, but heard no human voices. Thereupon, they pushed against the doors and opened the gates, following one another as they hurried inside. When they reached the palace courtyard, it was silent and empty of people; there were only skeletons. The officials and aides looked at one another in dismay, wailing and weeping, unable to fathom the source of the disaster. Siṃhala recounted the entire story from beginning to end, and the ministers and subjects believed him, realizing that the king had brought this disaster upon himself.  Thereupon, the state assistants, veteran ministers, various officials, and senior generals inquired after those of illustrious virtue and sought out those of sublime character; all admired the merit and wisdom of Siṃhala, and they consulted together, saying: "How can the one who rules the people be chosen haphazardly? He must first possess merit and wisdom, and secondly embody sagacity and discernment; for without merit and wisdom, one cannot enjoy the precious throne, and without sagacity and discernment, how can one manage the affairs of state? Siṃhala is the very man. He perceived the hidden danger in a dream, was moved by the response of the heavenly horse, was loyal in remonstrating with his lord, and was wise enough to protect himself. The mandate of history is here; let us compose a new song of praise." The masses were happy to support him and honored him by establishing him as king. Siṃhala, unable to decline the offer, agreed to hold to the middle path, and after bowing respectfully to the assembled officials, he ascended the throne. Thereupon, he reformed the previous abuses and set an example of virtue. He then issued an order, saying: "Our former merchant companions are in the land of the Rākṣasas; their life or death is uncertain, and good and evil are indistinguishable. Now, to rescue them from their plight, we should prepare our arms and armor; to save those in peril and show compassion to those in distress is a blessing to the state; to recover precious goods and store up treasures is a benefit to the state." Thereupon, he organized his troops and traveled across the sea. At that time, the banners of ill omen atop the iron city began to shake; the Rākṣasīs, seeing this, were struck with terror and immediately unleashed their seductive charms, coming out to meet the men to entice and deceive them. The king, having long known of their deceit, ordered his soldiers to recite mantras with their mouths and exert their martial might with their bodies. The Rākṣasīs stumbled, fell, and were defeated; some fled to hide on isolated islands, while others drowned in the surging currents. Thereupon, he destroyed the iron city, broke the iron prisons, rescued the merchants, and obtained many jewels. He recruited the common people to move and settle on the treasure island, established a capital, built towns, and thus a kingdom was formed. He then used the king’s name as the name of the country.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅) is a matter from a previous life of Śākya Tathāgata. In earlier times, the kingdom of Siṃhala only honored licentious sacrifices. In the hundredth year after the Buddha passed away, Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅), the younger brother of King Aśoka (無憂王), abandoned worldly desires to seek the fruits of sainthood; having attained the six supernatural powers and the eight liberations, he traveled through the air to this country to propagate the true Dharma and spread the bequeathed teachings. From that time onward, the customs have been pure and faithful. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas and over twenty thousand monks, who follow the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. More than two hundred years after the arrival of Buddhism, each [group] specialized in its own field, dividing into two schools: the first is the Mahāvihāra (摩訶毘訶羅) school, which rejects the Mahāyāna and studies the Lesser Vehicle; the second is the Abhayagiri (阿跋耶祇釐) school, which studies both vehicles and propagates the Tripiṭaka. The monks are pure in their moral conduct, their concentration and wisdom are clear and bright, their deportment is exemplary, and they are numerous and flourishing.  Beside the royal palace is the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth (佛牙精舍), several hundred feet high, shimmering with pearls and adorned with rare gems. A signal post is erected atop the temple, upon which is placed a large padmarāga jewel; its brilliant light shines resplendently, and when viewed from afar, it glitters like a bright star by day or night. Three times a day, the king bathes the Buddha’s tooth with scented water and powdered incense, either washing it or burning the incense, striving for the utmost rarity and splendor in his offerings.  Beside the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth is a small temple, which is also adorned and polished with various precious gems. Inside is a golden Buddha statue, cast by a former king of this country to be of equal stature to himself, with the uṣṇīṣa adorned with precious jewels. Later, there was a thief who waited for an opportunity to steal it, but the heavy doors and surrounding railings were guarded with strict vigilance. The thief then dug a tunnel to enter the temple through a hole; when he attempted to take the jewel, the statue gradually grew taller and higher. Having failed in his quest, the thief retreated and sighed, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata practiced the bodhisattva path, aroused a vast mind, and made great vows, offering up his own life and body, down to his cities and kingdoms, out of compassion for the four types of birth, bestowing everything upon all beings. Now, how could his bequeathed image be stingy with a jewel? Considered in this light, it does not make manifest his former conduct." The image then bowed its head and bestowed the jewel. Having obtained it, the thief immediately took it to sell. Those who saw it all said to him, "This treasure is the jewel from the *uṣṇīṣa* (頂髻) of the golden Buddha image of the former king. Where did you obtain it to come here and sell it?" They then seized him and reported it to the king. The king asked where he had obtained it, and the thief said, "The Buddha gave it to me himself; I am not a thief." The king, thinking he was not being truthful, ordered an envoy to go and verify it, and the image was still bowing its head. Witnessing this sacred miracle, the king’s faith became pure and firm; he did not punish the man, but instead redeemed the jewel at a high price, adorned the image’s *uṣṇīṣa*, and replaced it on the crown. Because of this, the image has remained with its head bowed until the present day.  Beside the royal palace, a great kitchen was built, preparing food for eighteen thousand monks daily. When the time for the meal arrived, the assembly of monks would hold their alms bowls to receive the provisions, and having received their food, each would return to his own residence. Since the time the Buddha’s teaching spread to this land, this offering was established, and descendants inherited the succession, continuing the practice until the present. For the past ten or more years, the country has been in political turmoil without a stable ruler, and this practice has been abandoned. The country is situated on the edge of the sea and the land produces precious gems. When the king personally performs sacrifices, the spirits present rare treasures. The city’s inhabitants and scholars travel back and forth to seek and collect them, and according to their karmic rewards, what they obtain differs. Depending on the pearls and gems they acquire, there is a set tax.

en_revised: Sailing several thousand *li* west across the sea from the country of Nārikela (那羅稽羅洲), on the eastern cliff of a solitary island, there is a stone Buddha statue over a hundred feet high, seated facing east. It has a moonstone (*candrakānta*) as its *uṣṇīṣa*; when the moon shines upon it, water flows down, drenching the cliffs and ridges and pouring into the mountain ravines. At one time, a group of merchants, having encountered a storm and drifted with the waves, arrived at this solitary island. The sea water was salty and undrinkable, and they suffered from thirst for a long time. It happened to be the fifteenth day of the month, and water flowed from the top of the statue, by which the entire group was saved; they believed that their utmost sincerity had moved the divine sage to rescue them. They remained there for several days, but whenever the moon was hidden behind the high cliffs, the water would not flow. The leader of the merchants then said, "It is not necessarily the case that it flows to save us. I have heard that when moonlight shines upon a moonstone, water will flow; could it be that there is such a gem atop the head of the Buddha statue?" They then climbed the cliff to look at it and found that the *uṣṇīṣa* of the image was indeed made of moonstone. I once met one of these men, who told the whole story from beginning to end.
li_quote: A man who had witnessed the event related the whole story.

en_revised: Traveling more than thirty *li* east from the battlefield, one arrives at the city of Pimo (媲摩城). There is a standing sandalwood Buddha image over two *zhang* in height. It possesses many miraculous powers and at times emits a brilliant light. Whenever people have illnesses, they apply gold leaf to the part of the image corresponding to their own area of pain, and they are immediately cured. Those who make requests with a sincere heart often have their wishes fulfilled. I heard the local people say: "This image was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王) of the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國) when the Buddha was still in the world. After the Buddha passed away, it traveled through the air from there to the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) in the north of this country." When it first arrived, the people of the city were peaceful and prosperous, but they were deeply attached to erroneous views and did not treasure or respect it; although they heard it had come of its own accord, they considered it divine but did not value it. Later, an Arhat came to pay homage to this image. The people of the city were shocked, finding his appearance and clothing strange, and they rushed to inform the king. The king then issued an order that this strange man should be covered with sand and earth. At that time, the Arhat was covered in sand and earth, and was left without any food to live on. There was one man whose heart could not bear this; he had long held this image in reverent worship, and upon seeing the Arhat, he secretly provided him with food. When the Arhat was about to depart, he said to the man: "Seven days from now, it will rain sand and earth, filling this city until not a single soul remains. You should know this and plan your escape early. It is because they covered me with sand that they have brought this calamity upon themselves." Having spoken, he departed and suddenly vanished. The man entered the city and told his relatives and friends in detail, but those who heard him did nothing but laugh and mock him. On the second day, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing away the filth and soil, and it rained various treasures that filled the streets; the people then berated their informant even more. This man, knowing in his heart that it was inevitable, secretly opened a tunnel, exited the city, and took shelter outside. On the night of the seventh day, after midnight, sand and earth rained down and filled the city. The man emerged from the tunnel and went east to this country, staying in the city of Bhīmā (嫓摩城). No sooner had the man arrived than the image also arrived; he immediately worshipped it there and dared not move it. According to ancient records, when the Dharma of Śākyamuni comes to an end, the image will enter the dragon palace. Today, the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) has become a great mound. Kings of various nations and powerful men from distant lands have often desired to excavate it to take its treasures, but as soon as they reach its vicinity, fierce winds suddenly arise, smoke and clouds gather from all sides, and the roads become lost.
li_quote: The arhat was covered with sand and earth and no food was provided to him.
